summary:
## Summary
Warm starts removed the optimizer failures. With measured noise, sv and fast guesses clearly improve held-out fit in
most mice; sz does not. Leak and urgency help only in the 3–4 mice with the most trials, so they fail parsimony rule 2
as written. The fast-only guess form (guess delay ≤ 0.3 s) is the best-supported guess form. The common model is not
chosen yet: the authors have to decide between strict rule 2 (L0U0V1Z0G1, fast-only guesses) and keeping leak and
urgency.

## Summary
Independently recomputed the control-strategy comparison and guess-bias score difference from saved fits, and
recomputed recovery rates and parameter correlations in memory. Incorporated these results into manuscript Results,
Abstract and Discussion, with uncertainty caveats. The independent pulse comparison remains pending: no primacy
output directory existed during this inspection, and no observed pulse outcomes were examined.

## Summary
Not power: the other seven mice pooled (12,307 trials) gain ~0 from leak (+6.8 ± 4.0) and urgency (−0.3 ± 4.5). In
the mice where they help, they mostly fit the rate of censored (> 5 s) trials. That rate is nearly
coherence-independent (5–12% even at 100%), yet the late responses are coherence-dependent (accuracy 0.57–0.88 by
coherence): consistent with a delayed start of integration, not disengagement. Neither model captures it.

## Summary
Read saved gate and strategy outputs and checked coverage counts and prediction commits. Both baselines fail
choice and RT adequacy; strategy test remains not distinguished under its original rule. Added these findings
to manuscript Results/Abstract/Discussion and withheld primacy claims. Amendment 6 is a draft, not adopted here.

## Summary
Created `dissemination/paper/manuscript_2026-10-22.md`: Introduction, established Results, Methods and bounded
Discussion prose, with pending strategy/timing sections and an incomplete abstract. Added source, paragraph-claim
and numeric-consistency records. Corrected censoring language in the existing captions and qualified the outline.
The parent paper plan remains active: scientific results, author facts, figures and final verification remain unfinished.

## Summary
All frozen prediction checksums match. Both strategies predict small and similar pulse effects. The completed
synthetic test rarely selects the generator with the primary pulse-specific statistic. Updated the manuscript
to distinguish control-trial model preference from limited independent pulse discrimination. No recorded pulse
choices or reaction times were read; no observed-analysis result files existed at the inspection.

## Summary
The pipeline works on synthetic data: predictions, gates, PyMC GLMMs and sensitivity jobs. No recorded pulse-trial
outcome was read. But the fitted DDM predicts that a ±100%, 50–67 ms pulse changes choices by only ~0.025 logit
(about 0.6 percentage points). Primacy can at most remove that effect, so the largest possible β_middle is ~0.03–0.04,
while the GLMM's standard error with all mice is ~0.05–0.07. Under the model as fitted, the confirmatory test cannot
detect primacy of any size. It becomes informative only if the observed pulse effects are much larger than the model
predicts, which is what the gate (step 6.2) checks.

## Summary
No to both. The revised gate fails for both baselines (departure +0.24 / +0.31 logit). The calibration shows the
procedure is valid under the null, but the timing test detects 0–5% of datasets with 10–40% primacy. Per amendment 6
item 8, the timing test is not run and no further revision is made. The data show a between-mouse-variable excess
pulse sensitivity, not an answer about primacy.

## Summary
The saved fits reproduce the table and reported medians/ranges. All ten fits have the expected common-model form, free guess bias, fifty simulation repetitions and warm starts. The boundary wording needs correction: the script flags proximity within 1% of the allowed parameter range, not exact boundary hits. Such estimates are potentially constrained; they are not established lower limits. Recommendation: retain the descriptive table, review fit quality and the ongoing diagnostics before prioritizing refits.

## Summary
Revised the Markdown manuscript around the agreed argument: control behaviour favours the tested accumulator, randomized pulses redirect choices, and the fitted models misplace the pulse effect in time. Added the assignment-based effect, pulse-aligned response curves, stimulus audit, model diagnostics and corresponding Methods. Preserved the original/revised failed gates, low strategy sensitivity and the decision not to run the confirmatory timing test. The tau-p pilot remains outside formal claims pending its planned independent check.

## Summary
Retain the accessible comparative motivation, direction-to-lick task illustration, psychometric introduction and pulse-coherence traces. Replace the poster's accumulation/primacy assertions with the current model comparison, assignment-based pulse effect and predictive limitations. Updated the story document and caption production notes; formal numerical captions are unchanged. The WFV experiment remains outside this paper.

## Summary
- Positive (rightward) vs negative (leftward) scheduled pulses, primary set (|coh| ≤ 36%): **Δdirection = +5.84 pp, 95% t CI [1.80, 9.89], n = 10 mice**. Unadjusted p = 0.0097, Holm p = 0.019. Mouse bootstrap [2.60, 9.16].
- Components: ΔR +4.81 [0.47, 9.16], ΔL −6.88 [−10.97, −2.78], Δunresponded +2.07 [−0.36, 4.49]. Mostly a redirection of responses, possibly with a small increase in omissions under positive pulses (t CI includes 0).
- Positive vs control: Δdirection +4.86 [2.43, 7.29], Holm p = 0.0043. Control vs negative: +1.40 [−2.13, 4.92], Holm p = 0.39. All three Holm family members were estimable.
- The direction is consistent across leave-one-mouse-out, session halves, within-session halves and the pseudo-onset seed sensitivity. Zero coherence and matched seeds point the same way but are imprecise. 9 of 10 mice have positive Δdirection.
- Confidence: moderate for a nonzero directional effect of a few pp. Low for its size (wide CI with n = 10) and for any pulse-sign asymmetry.

Assignment was verified as randomized and unannounced (cfg assignment_verdict). So the positive-vs-negative assignment contrast can be worded causally, with that verdict's two qualifications: the task code read is the repository HEAD, and there are small outcome-dependent exclusions. Pulse vs control additionally depends on pseudo-onsets for UCLA controls, which D1 accepted.

## Summary
The contract is frozen: run `20261023T191030Z_fa8de8b`, config v2, `ready_for_behaviour = true`, and all 21 checks
pass. The user supplied the task source code mid-session. It shows that **assignment is randomized and unannounced in
both rigs, conditional on coherence** (UW: independent per-trial draws; UCLA: permuted blocks). Causal wording for the
assignment contrast is therefore supported, with the qualifications listed under Caveats. A found one label bug in
the existing DDM inputs (48 trials), one outcome-dependent exclusion (15 trials) and one UW design asymmetry. All
three are now explicit in the contract. Confidence is high for the identity, label and censoring facts (checked
mechanically), and moderate for the code-version match to collection.

## Summary
- **The decomposition is exact.** The objective splits into three parts: response vs censored, choice given response, and RT bins.
- **A choice–RT tradeoff is demonstrated in the two mice with the most data and an RT term that covers almost all trials.** In PSUIM6 and PSUIM7, the gain that best fits choices (4–7) is 2–3× the joint optimum. The RT term rejects that gain, both in-sample and on held-out folds. In 6 of the other 8 mice the choice term is too flat to tell.
- **The mismatch is in the timing of the pulse's directional effect.** At every gain the model puts the directional effect early (0–1 s after onset) and then reverses part of it. The data show no early effect, accrual at 0.5–2 s and no reversal. This holds for the leak/urgency baseline too.
- **No common latency effect needs explaining.** The model at the fitted gains predicts almost none, and neither do the data (package D).
- **The with/against-coherence asymmetry from amendment 6 matches the control fit's own coherence-slope error.** It is the known control psychometric misfit, not a pulse effect.
- **Physical amplitude errors are too small.** Package B allows at most ×1.4, while the choice data need ×2–7. B's rounding shift accounts for at most about 0.3 pp.
- **Recommendation:** one bounded candidate, an added causal pulse time constant (F branch 1 form; B gives it no physical support). It has explicit falsifiers, and benchmarking on PSUIM6/PSUIM7 should come before anything wider.
- **Confidence:** moderate for the timing mismatch and for the tradeoff in PSUIM6 and PSUIM7; low elsewhere.

## Summary
Recommend a versioned input correction and the reduced exploratory pilot, with the safeguards below; this recommendation is not authorization to execute it. The behavioural result already supports a substantive thesis contribution. A temporal-filter pilot tests a specific predictive repair, not a neural mechanism. Several claims in E overstate what the stimulus audit and null behavioural contrasts establish.

## Summary
Drafted a shared trial/assignment contract followed by parallel stimulus, directional-behaviour and joint-response workstreams. Existing-model diagnosis determines whether a narrowly bounded candidate is worth implementing. The behavioural Results package can be completed independently of mechanism identification. Only documentation was created or updated; no workers, analyses or jobs were launched.

## Summary
- **D1 accepted.** UW uses recorded sham onsets. UCLA uses A's fixed-seed pseudo-onsets, which are reproduced exactly from metadata and match the pulse-onset distribution. The grid is 0 to 4.58 s since onset, a common range inside every trial's follow-up.
- **Direction.** Pulses redirect responses. For pooled strata in the onset-eligible set, the directional contrast (dR - dL)/2 (positive minus negative) is +5.85 pp at u = 4.58 s, 95% t-interval [1.93, 9.77] across 10 mice. It is positive in 8 of 10 mice.
- **Timing of the directional mass.** It accumulates mainly between 0.5 and 2 s after onset, which is where most responses occur. It is about 0 before 0.5 s.
- **Latency and response rate.** I found no clear common effect of both pulse signs against control on response rate or latency (for example, -0.51 pp responded by 4.58 s, [-2.10, 1.09]). With 10 mice the study is underpowered, so this null should not be over-read.
- **Confidence.** Moderate for the direction effect. Everything else is low and descriptive: intervals are pointwise, with no multiplicity correction.

## Summary
- The replay is internally consistent. Before onset the rendered frames and the ME are bitwise identical with and
  without the pulse in all 532 replays. The ME is causal: it first differs one frame after the stimulus does. The
  replay reproduces the stored ME and the DDM's S+N. VERIFIED.
- Returning to baseline redraws every noise-dot direction. This is in the task code itself, not only in the replay.
  After the pulse the noise is a new, independent draw (pre/post noise correlation about 0). Its pulse-aligned mean
  is about 0, so it adds noise but no directional bias. VERIFIED.
- A small directional bias does exist, and it is deterministic. Rounding in the task's coherence-update code leaves
  one more or one fewer coherent dot after the return, always toward the pulse direction, and this lasts for the rest
  of the trial. The size is +0.198% coherence (UCLA |c| = 9 congruent, 18 and 36 incongruent) and +0.658% (UW |c| = 9
  and 36 incongruent). Averaged over all genuine pulses that is +0.074% (UCLA) and +0.161% (UW). VERIFIED in code and
  in all 13,547 pulse trials checked. Whether it matters for behaviour is a HYPOTHESIS for C/E.
- The UCLA replay's one-frame freezes cut its early pulse energy. The replay gives 72–78% of the 0–333 ms pulse
  energy of the no-freeze and display-loop alternatives (ratios 1.28 to 1.40). Which alternative matches acquisition
  is UNKNOWN. For UW the task frame-counter convention and the replay agree within 1%.
- Recommendation: a full physical-omission replay is not needed to interpret the existing behaviour. If the pulse gain
  is reported quantitatively, recompute the UCLA pulse with labelled alternatives. Cost is about 46 core-hours per
  convention (≈ 5.7 h on 8 cores).

## Summary
**FAIL under the frozen rule. Modelling stops.** A slower pulse response (tau_p = 300 ms, the grid edge) improves the
joint fit in both mice, in sample and in 4 of 5 held-out folds each. It does **not** bring the choice and RT gains
together, and it does **not** remove the late reversal. Criteria P2 and P3 fail in both mice. The frozen P0 check
flagged float32 rounding; that does not affect the decision (see the P0 finding). Confidence that the candidate does
not fix the mismatch in these two mice: moderate to high. Generality: low, because only 2 mice from one rig were tested.

## Summary
Completed a targeted primary-literature review and read-only pipeline/data audit. Recommend adjusted directional
pulse effects and pulse-aligned joint choice–RT distributions, then stimulus validation and a small exploratory
model comparison conditional on recoverability. Existing primacy stopping rules remain intact. The user explicitly
ruled out new behavioural data. Detailed synthesis: `dissemination/reports/pulse-thesis-research-2026-10-23.md`;
public search/source record: `dissemination/reports/pulse-thesis-searches-2026-10-23.json`.

## Summary
- **C's Student-t interval across mice is adequate:** coverage is 0.93–0.975 in all six scenarios.
- **The mouse bootstrap percentile interval under-covers:** coverage is 0.85–0.925.
- **Null rejection is at or below nominal:** the primary test rejects 0.025 of the time (95% MC CI [0.008, 0.057]); the Holm family rejects 0.030 [0.011, 0.064].
- **Power of the primary test (unadjusted / Holm):**
  - δ = 3 pp: 0.29 / 0.21
  - δ = 6 pp: 0.81 / 0.64
  - δ = 10 pp: 0.995 / 0.985
- **Estimator behaviour:** C and D are unbiased to within Monte Carlo error. Probability conservation, the CIF checks, censoring and the rule that pre-onset responses are unaffected held in all 1,200 datasets. D recovers a known time-local perturbation, and C recovers a censoring-driven change in response rate.
- **Confidence:** high for the estimator and censoring logic. Moderate for interval calibration, because it depends on the assumed outcome model and normal heterogeneity across mice.

## Summary
Drafted a story that connects the control-trial preference for the tested accumulator to a model-independent directional pulse effect and a specific temporal prediction failure. Proposed five main figures, merging the old stimulus/hidden-coherence displays to give two main figures to pulses. Wrote complete proposed main captions, production notes and alt text, with supplementary content briefs. The new files preserve the existing manuscript/captions and do not incorporate an unevaluated model pilot.

## Summary
VERIFIED: a four-shard public-source search, independent metadata audit, synthesis and adversarial scoop check produced 35 verified sources. An author-requested mouse-specific fact-check then added nine unique verified precedents, producing a 44-source ledger. Broad mouse novelty is false: continuous RDK, dynamic visual evidence accumulation and visual DDM/RT modelling were already established separately. No retained source performed the exact control-fit to randomized signed-motion-pulse transfer test across choice, response probability and response-time distributions.

## Summary
(a) No. 40% gain decay moves the stimulus-aligned primacy index by ~0.1 % coh against a per-dataset SD of ~0.6; group
detection 0-5%. (b) Yes at the group level. A response-aligned late-weight index classifies 20/20 integrator and
20/20 extrema-detection datasets correctly (criterion >= 90%). Per mouse, only PSUIM6/7 (~3,200 trials) are reliably
classified (100%); the others are at 25-90%. Confidence: moderate. See the caveats (no refit; only two candidate models).

## Summary
VERIFIED: yes. The revised outline assigns all 21 approved claims exactly once, gives each main figure one headline, mirrors Results and Methods, and budgets 4,980 words for the eLife main text. An independent reviewer precommitted 12 criteria, requested three bounded revisions, and passed the revised package with no remaining P0/P1/P2 issues. G3 now awaits author approval.

## Summary
PARTLY. Figure legends passed, and Methods passed statistical review, but Methods and Results did not both receive full PASS after two rounds. No new analysis is required. One approved-claim inconsistency must be corrected: C007 requires secondary-pipeline gate outcomes that the Methods brief did not define. Human authorization is required before a narrowly scoped third review round.

## Summary
Yes. A versioned Results v4 now follows a question-to-result narrative while retaining the locked thesis, all seven
approved Results claims and all 42 registered number tokens. No analysis, estimate or scientific conclusion changed.
The canonical section is 2,746/2,850 words and all deterministic Results checks pass without warnings.

## Summary
Five notebooks now wrap the tested modules in `scripts/paper/`, prepare shared data once, and give every labeled panel its own Markdown heading and code cell. Figures 1–2 expose panels A–E; Figures 3–5 expose panels A–D. All five notebooks execute successfully with the project virtual environment. Source notebooks retain no outputs and contain no export calls, so running them cannot overwrite the selected artwork.

## Summary
Pre-specified verdict: **neither model fits**. S_I = 11.44 just exceeds its 95th-percentile reference (11.22) and S_E =
14.74 exceeds its reference (13.21). The data lie nominally closer to the integrator, but by the frozen rule this is
inconclusive and does not qualify as supporting evidence for the accumulation-first paper (author condition: "add it if
it pans out"). Confidence in the verdict itself: high (deterministic, rule fixed in advance).

## Summary
Figures 1 and 2 are assembled, visually inspected and selected as versioned PDF/SVG/300-dpi PNG exports. Figure 1
uses mice for behavioural summaries and retains no-response trials explicitly; Figure 2 uses trials/seeds/replay
conventions and never presents stimulus dispersion as across-mouse uncertainty. Exact source tables accompany every
selected panel. The selected five-figure set, captions and neuropaper legends are reconciled, with no unresolved claim
or number tokens and no main-figure `[MISSING]` markers.

## Summary
Figures 3–5 are assembled as versioned PDF, SVG and 300-dpi PNG files with adjacent source-data CSVs. Figure 3 keeps
held-out model comparisons separate from descriptive in-sample fit quality. Figures 4–5 make the randomized behavioural
pulse effect and the model's temporal mismatch the visual centre of the paper. No fitting or cluster work was run.

## Summary
VERIFIED: all six neuropaper sections are `passed`. Introduction v2 and title/abstract v2 each passed independent round-2 review after bounded revisions, and the full deterministic check has zero errors. G4 is written but not approved. Three Methods reproducibility-table placeholders became stale when the selected Figure 1–3 audits were completed; G4 proposes an exact evidence-only N105–N107 patch before assembly rather than silently carrying those placeholders forward.

## Summary
VERIFIED: G4 was approved with the bounded N105–N107 Methods patch. The S5 manuscript was assembled with a
repository-local, marker-aware renderer because the pinned neuropaper renderer duplicated units for compound ledger
records. Independent coherence review found no scientific drift and specified eight bounded editorial repairs; those
repairs are applied and all contract checks pass. Supplementary Figure S6 v2 is selected, visually inspected and backed
by one adjacent source CSV per panel. It reports failed original and gain-revised gates, low frozen-strategy sensitivity,
low timing-test sensitivity and the resulting stopping sequence; it is not a null result for temporal weighting.

## Summary
*k* = 5/20, so under the D002 rule **THESIS_B** applies: the comparison favored the accumulator on real data but also
on a quarter of E-generated datasets, so it does not reliably distinguish the two strategies. The 5 are not optimizer
failures: in each, C's held-out NLL is lower than E's at E's own generating parameters (by 15-80). Confidence in k:
high for these 20 datasets; k itself has binomial uncertainty (2 replicates x 10 mice).

## Summary
The data contradict the censoring assumption for most of these trials: non-response stays high at 100% coherence,
rises steeply at the end of sessions and comes in runs. This matches lapse/disengagement states, not unfinished
diffusion. Effects on the fits are SUSPECTED, not tested; the responded-only refits (src-85) will test them.

## Summary
No asymmetry: excluding asymmetric UW cells, observed incongruent - congruent = 0.54 ± 3.22 pp (p 0.87); every model
predicts 0.36-0.84 pp; observed minus model ≈ 0 for all 7 (Holm p 1.0). The 2.0 vs 4.0 pp split in the earlier figure
came with the asymmetric cells. The test is weak (95% CI of the difference about ±7 pp). At ±100% the excess pulse-direction
errors (3.77 ± 1.15 pp per trial) are spread over RTs, largest at 1-2 s; not concentrated in the fast-guess range.

## Summary
They hold and get slightly larger. Positive vs negative pulse: 5.84 pp [1.80, 9.89] -> 7.52 pp [2.73, 12.30],
p 0.0097 -> 0.0062 (Holm over the 3 contrasts: 0.019 -> 0.012). The pulse does not significantly change the
response rate (+2.07 pp, p = 0.086), so conditioning on responding is unlikely to drive the effect. Model fits,
gates and calibration are not covered here (refits needed; src-85 owns the refits).

## Summary
Inconclusive, and this design cannot settle it. Pulses always go to +-100%, so within |c| <= 36 |D| only spans 64-136%.
The two hypotheses then predict effects that differ by ~0.12 logit across the range, below the per-arm uncertainty. The
overall pulse effect is clear (0.17 logit, p 0.009); its dependence on |D| is not resolved either way.

## Summary
Not a calculation bug. The difference is the filter change of 2026-10-13 (dissemination/reports/motion-energy-methods.md §2.2-2.3, §3.1-3.2).
Stimulus replay and pulse placement are identical on master and this branch. The old filter is non-causal (centred padding,
unflipped kernels, 6-frame temporal window), so its pulse response starts about 1 frame before onset and peaks at about 0-17 ms with
height close to the nominal change. The new causal mouse filter (k 34 /s, 0.55 s) delays the response (rise ~50 ms, peak ~120 ms) and spreads it over ~300 ms
(peak about 1/3 of nominal, area ratio 0.99; see refit plan log).

## Summary
All seven variants predict pulse effects of 0.35-1.9 pp, below the observed ones (congruent 2.0 pp, incongruent 4.0 pp,
|c| <= 36). Adding a cross-validated pulse gain or using ES gets closest but still predicts about half the incongruent effect.
Observed effects are noisy per coherence (SEM 1-6 pp), so the per-coherence shape is not informative. Descriptive only.

## Summary
None of the three expectations holds. The pulse effect is in fast-to-middle RTs (median ~0.5-1.3 s) and absent in the
two slowest quintiles; slow ±100% control trials are the most accurate (0.91), the fast ones the least (0.66); and
pulse-direction choices are faster on pulse trials (median -71 ms, 0.9 quantile -152 ms; noisy). This pattern looks more
like the pulse acting as evidence on trials still deciding shortly after it than like a readout bias on slow trials. Descriptive; exploratory.

## Summary
The model gets the shape right: pulse effect in fast-to-middle RTs, none in slow ones, pulse-direction choices faster,
control accuracy rising with RT. It falls short in magnitude in Q1-Q3 (median RT ~0.45-1.3 s), and it predicts a small
late reversal (Q5, -1.6 to -1.8 pp) that the data do not show. Only one bin survives correction (±100% Q2, +8.2 pp).
So the gap is a too-weak pulse on trials deciding within ~1 s of the pulse, not a different mechanism visible in RT.

## Summary
Not after correction. Pooled over stages, congruent pulses shift choices toward the pulse by 3.0 pp [0.3, 5.8]
(8/10 mice, dz 0.80, Holm p 0.096) and incongruent by 3.6 pp [-2.2, 9.4] (7/10, Holm p 0.39); they do not differ
(-0.5 pp, p 0.87). Each is roughly half of the positive-vs-negative contrast (7.52 pp, Holm 0.012), which pools both
directions and does not subtract the noisier control cells. Per-stage tests are all non-significant (late: 6 mice).

## Summary
Pulses act on bias, not slope. Right minus left bias: early -17.1% coherence (Holm 0.047), middle -12.4 (p 0.021,
Holm 0.10), late -16.8 with a CI spanning zero (6 mice). No slope difference at any time. Only the early bias
difference survives correction, narrowly; the 6-test family was set after the 36-test results were seen, so treat the
corrected p values as post hoc.

## Summary
Two of 36 tests survive Holm, both early pulses: congruent curves are steeper than incongruent ones (slope +0.040 per %
coherence, Holm 0.022), and right pulses shift the bias leftward (-15.1% coherence, Holm 0.011) while left pulses do not
shift it (+2.0, Holm 1.0). Middle pulses point the same way but nothing survives; late pulses (6 mice) show nothing.
The slope contrast congruent - incongruent asks the same question as positive-vs-negative (do choices follow the pulse),
not the pp "congruent - incongruent" asymmetry, which was ~1 pp and n.s.

## Summary
No within-mouse evidence that the pulse effect changes with pulse time. Every within-mouse contrast (early - middle on
10 mice; early - late, middle - late on the 6 mice with late pulses) has an interval spanning zero, in the per-mouse
tests, the hierarchical model, and the RT-conditioned sensitivity. The apparent decline in per-stage group means
(early > middle > late) is mostly a mouse-set effect: late pulses exist only in 6 mice, and those mice have small
pulse effects at every pulse time. Underpowered: a modest decline cannot be excluded.

## Summary
No. Within one dataset, the number of responded synthetic trials (n_train / n_test) differs between candidates in many
datasets, so their held-out NLLs come from different trials and the "C - E" style differences that recovery is scored on
are not paired. This affects the full matrix and the existing pairwise recoveries, including F1a k = 5/20 (THESIS_B under
D002) and the ESx/DDMx and ES recoveries. Those results should be treated as invalid until rerun on fixed datasets.
Likely cause (SUSPECTED): synthesis runs on the GPU (torch.randn), whose draws for a given seed depend on the GPU model;
jobs ran on mixed hardware (A100 lab pool and ckpt-all).

## Summary
They are barely distinguishable. On held-out control trials DDMx is better than ESx by > 10 in 3/10 mice, ESx in none
(summed 62.7); the pulse strategy test does not distinguish them at any of three pulse latencies; and recovery is weak
(each model's own data recognised in 5-7/20, 12/20 within 10). Both fit far worse than C (summed 655-718, C better in
6/10 mice, neither better in any). Conclusion consistent with F1a (THESIS_B): without drift variability and fast
guesses, neither strategy model captures these mice, and these data do not separate the two strategies.

## Summary
The analysed data are 50 of 298 sessions (17%) from 10 of 14 mice; every session had pulses, so 77% of responded pulse
trials sit in excluded sessions. Exclusion uses control-trial behaviour only, so it is valid, but it is strict. Five
findings matter for modelling: (1) choices after the 5 s deadline (14% of trials, excluded) are as accurate as on-time
choices, so they are not disengaged guesses; (2) RTs are floored at 0.3 s with a pile-up there and low accuracy below
0.5 s (a fast-guess population); (3) choice history moves choices about as much as the pulse (repeat-the-last-choice
after errors in 8/10 mice); (4) no-response rises through the session (9/10 mice); (5) the pulse effect is stable across
sessions within a mouse (no heterogeneity, no trend) and the mice that ignore it in included sessions also ignore it in
excluded sessions.

## Summary
On 14,014 responded control trials from 10 mice, RT falls weakly with coherence and errors are faster than correct
responses. The motion-energy kernel is small (about 0.1-0.3% coherence) and, with these trial counts, cannot be
distinguished from 0 or from either model. Within-mouse simulation SD (0.2-1.1) is as large as the predicted kernel
(about 0.3-0.5), so the kernel analysis is underpowered. The common model under-predicts fast errors (exploratory).
Paired recovery datasets now exist (80, CPU, sha256); the 320-fit rerun awaits submission by the author.

## Summary
`scripts/ddm/control_heldout.py` reproduces paper_accumulation heldout_per_trial_2026-10-28 exactly. The common model's
advantage is mostly in the RT terms. Against ES, ESx and DDMx the choice part is about 0 and not significant. Against
rapid forgetting (E) there is a small, consistent choice advantage (2.5 per 1,000 trials, positive in 10/10 mice). The
group results survive dropping any one mouse.

## Summary
Both of their behavioural analyses run on our data and give the same qualitative picture: a pulse shifts the
psychometric function by a fixed coherence equivalent, with no separate effect on RT, and it affects choices made from
about 0.3 s after pulse onset onward, not earlier. Differences: the shift is much larger in coherence units (12% vs
1.6%), the effect lasts to about 1.2-1.8 s after the pulse and then fades, and pulses change the RT distribution shape
slightly (KS p < .001, D 0.03-0.04) where theirs did not. The diffusion fit to mean RT is poor in mice, so per-mouse
k, A and t_nd are not interpretable; gamma is carried by the choices.

## Summary
Adding pulse trials to the fit changes almost nothing. The ranking is the control-only one (L1U1 best in the sum, but
beyond 10 NLL in only 2/10 mice; urgency alone drops behind the primary model). The primary model's parameters stay at
~1.0x its control-only fit, so the earlier UCLA parameter shift (known issue) does not reproduce and looks like a flat
likelihood ridge. No family reproduces the size of the pulse effect: every one predicts 2.3-4.5 pp in the 0.3-1.2 s
window against 5.48 pp in the data, and none reaches the 10-16 pp of PSUIM5/6/7 or DBM6. The predicted late reversal
is a property of drift variability and leak, not of integration: families without sv, and the extrema and Stine
models, predict none. High confidence on the descriptive results; the mechanism of the reversal is SUSPECTED.

## Summary
Nothing. The likelihood (CensoredQMLE, src/ddm/likelihood_calculator_censored.py) scores per condition the choice counts and
the RT quantiles per choice. On control trials, condition = signed coherence (build_ddm_inputs.py line 149). So
predictions are pooled over the trials of a condition, and no trial's choice is matched to its own stimulus. Shuffling the
noise between trials of the same coherence leaves the likelihood unchanged up to Monte Carlo noise. The shuffled-ME refit
is a no-op by construction and should not be run. The input enters only through the distribution of stimuli within a
condition, which acts like between-trial drift variability. The only trial-level test of motion-energy use is the kernel,
which is null and underpowered (reports/2026-10-29-control-descriptives.md).

## Summary
The pulse effect lives in responses made 0.3 to 1.2 s after the pulse: 5.5 pp [0.8, 10.2] over 10 mice (t p 0.027,
Holm 0.08 over 3; logit 0.24 [0.01, 0.47], Holm 0.12). After 1.2 s the effect is 1.2 pp [-2.8, 5.2], so there is
no group-level reversal, but the interval admits a small one. The effect is carried by 5 mice (PSUIM5/6/7, DBM5, DBM6);
the 5 sparsest mice are near zero. The "no reversal" pattern is clear only in PSUIM6/7; DBM6 does reverse (late window
-3.4 to -7.2 pp in each stage, SE about 6 to 9 pp per bin). Toward-pulse choices are faster mainly in the slow tail, and
their RT SD shrinks after middle pulses. No coherence dependence of the onset effect is detectable. Moderate confidence
in S1 window results; S2 and the late-stage parts of S3 are underpowered.

## Summary
1. Nothing already in hand decides it. The three descriptive pulse results (no within-mouse change across onsets;
   effect present for responses within ~1.2 s of the pulse and absent later; toward-pulse choices faster) are what a
   fixed-bound integrator with bound depletion, non-decision time and drift variability produces; leak and urgency
   change them only per undecided trial, in the second-order structure. The literature report gives the sources.
2. The pulses do carry information at the project's trial counts: in the two dense mice a leak of 1 /s or more moves the
   pulse-to-response profile (S1) away from the leak-free model by 2 to 10 bootstrap SE in the 0.6 to 1.2 s bins, and
   urgency of 3 /s by 2 to 3.5 SE. Urgency of 0.3 /s (the control-fitted range) moves it by under 1.6 SE and is not
   resolvable; urgency of 1 /s is marginal (0.5 to 2.5 SE). Stop rule SR1 (feasibility) is therefore not triggered.
3. But no member of the family, with or without leak or urgency, reproduces the observed profile: the data hold a flat
   13 to 19 pp effect across 0.3 to 1.2 s and ~0 afterwards, whereas every variant peaks in the first bin, is near 0 by
   0.9 to 1.2 s (3.5 to 9 SE below the data in PSUIM7) and reverses to -8 to -24 pp after 1.2 s. Leak makes the
   mismatch worse; mild urgency does not repair it. Within the family the data sit on the "no leak" side of the
   leak-free model, so leak >= 1 /s is disfavoured, but only conditionally on a family that fails SR4 (falsification).
4. Route: the leak-versus-urgency answer has to come from a joint fit of (L, u, pulse gain w) with the non-decision
   time pinned, judged first by ex-post reproduction of S1 to S3 and only second by held-out likelihood, after a recovery
   grid on the real schedules. The illustration predicts the fit will fail SR4 before it reaches L versus u, so the
   first modelling target is the sustained-then-absent pulse response, not leak or urgency. Details in "Route" below.
All simulation numbers here are an exploratory illustration (parameters re-matched on a coarse grid, three mice), not a
fit and not a power analysis.

Removing the freeze raises the UCLA pulse template by 1.13x (0-333 ms sum) to 1.15x (peak). The UW/UCLA pulse

## Summary

## Summary
- The mean early effect (5.48 pp) is uncertain: 95% CI 3.2-7.9 pp. Motion-energy integrators (3.3-5.3) lie inside
  it, so "integrators predict too small a mean effect" (reports/2026-11-09-mapping-accumulator-exploratory.md) is NOT
  established by the mean alone; only nominal-input integrators and ME urgency (2.3-3.1) fall below the CI.
- The per-mouse spread is real: Cochran's Q 51.7 on 9 df (p < 0.001, I^2 0.83) early; 21.0 (p 0.013, I^2 0.57) late.
  No family captures it: early chi-square over mice 77-177 on 10 df for all 28 families.
- The late mean (+1.22 pp, CI -1.0 to 3.4) excludes the reversal of the leak/urgency integrators (-1.3 to -2.9) but not
  that of the plain sv integrators (nominal primary -0.86, control-only primary -1.02). The strongest late misfits are
  leak+urgency under power and norm (chi-square 35 on 10 df). So the late reversal is mainly a leak/urgency problem;
  sv alone is not clearly inconsistent with the data at 1.2-5 s.

## Summary

## Summary
- Fitting pulse trials alone does not fix the pulse misfit. The per-mouse spread of the early effect stays unexplained
  (chi-square 91-140 on 10 df, as for all-trial fits 100-143), and with sv the late reversal remains (-1.0 to -2.9 pp
  vs data +1.2). By the plan's reading these are structural for these families, not a control-vs-pulse tension.
- The early mean effect rises a little (4.2-5.2 pp with sv vs 3.1-4.2 all-trial), inside the data CI (3.2-7.9).
- Without sv, pulse-only fits match both window means (early 3.8-5.1, late +0.7 to +1.2; data 5.5 and 1.2) but have
  worse held-out NLL on pulse trials in every pair (+25 to +68, carried by 1-3 mice) and predict controls worse
  (+159 to +587).
- Pulse-trial parameters differ consistently from all-trial ones: longer non-decision time (ndt higher in 6-9/10 mice
  per family) and more fast guesses (p_guess higher in 5-8/10). Moderately confident (descriptive, 10 mice).

## Summary
- Given leak 2-20 /s and urgency 0-50 /s, the fits leave the UGM corner: 0 of 120 full-data fits are in it (leak 4-10
  and urgency >= 1); 14 of 720 fits are, all pulse-only CV folds, 9 of them PSUIM10 (fewest trials). Fits sit at
  the edge nearest the standard model (median tau 400-495 ms, median urgency 0.00-0.71 /s).
- So the criteria end up testing that edge, not the corner itself. On it: with sv, NLL within 10 of the best
  integrator in 5-7/10 mice, but every with-sv family has a late reversal outside the data CI (criterion 2 fails).
  Without sv, the late window is inside the CI but NLL is within 10 in only 3/10 mice (joint) or 6-7/10 (pulse-only).
- No UGM family passes both criteria in most mice; the corner proper is ruled out to the extent the optimizer's
  avoidance shows (moderately confident: it is not a profile likelihood over the corner).

## Summary
Full-data bits (fits scored on their training trials, independent seed) rank all-trial models like rescored BIC
(Spearman 0.94) and are useful descriptively. Held-out bits (CV test folds scored by their fold's fit) are dominated by
Monte Carlo noise at 150 reps: a second seed moves family means by 5-26 mbits, as much as the model gaps. They do not
rank models reliably and should not replace held-out NLL. Confidence: high on the noise finding (two seeds), moderate on
the full-data ranking (single seed, 30 reps; bias check at more reps not done).
